content.title: FOOD FACTS THAT SOUND MADE UP BUT ARE 100% TRUE
facts: **Nutmeg** contains a natural compound called myristicin — in large enough doses it's actually a hallucinogen, which is why it's regulated as a controlled substance in some countries when concentrated.
**Cashews** are never sold in their shell to consumers because the shell contains a resin closely related to the one in poison ivy — it can blister skin on contact.
**Strawberries** aren't technically berries, but bananas are. Botanically, a true berry needs seeds formed inside the flesh from a single ovary, which bananas meet and strawberries don't.
**Apples** float in water because roughly 25% of their volume is air pockets in the flesh — that's also why bobbing for apples actually works.
**Carrots** were originally purple, not orange. Orange carrots were bred by Dutch growers centuries ago, and that variety simply became the commercial standard.
**Almonds** are technically seeds from a fruit closely related to peaches — the fuzzy fruit around them is usually discarded before it ever reaches a store.
**Rhubarb** stalks are edible, but its leaves contain enough oxalic acid to cause serious poisoning if eaten in quantity — it's one of the only common vegetables with a genuinely toxic part.

caption:
The nutmeg fact still gets people every time — the compound is called myristicin, and your liver actually has to metabolize it into a psychoactive substance before any effect kicks in, which is why it takes a large dose and hours to feel anything. The cashew one is real too: cashews are botanically related to poison ivy and mangoes (the same plant family, Anacardiaceae), which is exactly why the raw shells are burned off or steamed before you ever see a bag of them in a store. And the carrot story is genuinely historical — wild carrots came in purple, white, and yellow long before the orange variety we know today became dominant. Everyone's body reacts a little differently to compounds like these, so always go with properly prepared, store-bought versions.
